blurb: How a model learns by guessing the next word trillions of times, what it reads, and why bigger reliably means better.

cards.title: How a chatbot first learns: guess the next word

steps.p: A brand-new model is billions of numbers set at random. Ask it anything and it replies with gibberish. Pretraining is the long process that fills those numbers with knowledge.
steps.analogy: A newborn's brain: all the wiring is there, but none of the knowledge yet.

steps.p: Take a sentence from the internet, hide the next word, and ask the model to guess it. It doesn't pick one word — it gives a probability to every word it knows.

visual.caption: The model's guesses for: "The cat sat on the ___"

steps.p: The real next word was "mat". Training nudges all the model's numbers very slightly, so "mat" would get a bit more probability next time. Then it moves on to the next word.
The right answer is simply whatever word actually came next, so nobody has to mark anything. That's why this is called self-supervised learning: the text marks its own homework.
steps.analogy: Reading a book with your hand over the next line, guessing it, then peeking to check.

steps.h: Why guessing words makes it smart
steps.p: To guess well across all kinds of writing, the model has to pick up grammar, facts and patterns of reasoning — because each of those makes the next word easier to predict.
steps.analogy: To guess the last line of a detective novel ("The killer was…"), you have to have followed the whole plot.

cards.aside: Every chatbot you've used started life this way: as a very, very good next-word guesser.

cards.q: In pretraining, where does the "right answer" for each guess come from?
options: The word that actually came next in the text
A human teacher who marks each guess
A second AI that grades every answer
A dictionary built into the model
cards.why: The text itself. Every word in every document is a free practice question: the words before it are the question, the word itself is the answer. That's why no one has to label anything by hand.

cards.q: The model guesses: mat 41%, floor 22%, sofa 15%. The real next word was "sofa". What does training do?
options: Nudges the numbers so "sofa" gets a bit more probability next time
Deletes "mat" from the model's vocabulary
Nothing — the model was close enough
Changes the text so "mat" becomes correct
cards.hint: Training always moves the model a little toward the real answer.
cards.why: A small nudge toward the truth. Every guess gives a tiny correction. One nudge does almost nothing; trillions of them add up to a model that writes fluently.

cards.title: Meta's Llama 3 was pretrained on over 15 trillion tokens of text.
cards.detail: A token is about ¾ of a word, so that's roughly 11 trillion words. Reading nonstop at 250 words a minute, one person would need over 80,000 years to get through it.

visual.caption: Each new generation reads several times more text.

cards.statement: A model fresh out of pretraining (a "base model") behaves like a helpful chatbot.
cards.hint: Pretraining only teaches it to continue text.
cards.why: False. A base model just continues text. Ask "What's the capital of France?" and it may reply with more quiz questions, because that's what often follows such a line online. Being a helpful assistant is taught later, in post-training.

cards.q: Why would guessing the next word teach a model facts?
options: Text that mentions facts is easier to predict if you know them
Facts are stored in a separate database the model reads
The model is told which sentences are true
It doesn't — models never pick up facts this way
cards.hint: Try finishing: "The Eiffel Tower is in…"
cards.why: Knowing facts makes text predictable. To fill in "The Eiffel Tower is in ___", it helps enormously to have absorbed "Paris". Over trillions of words many facts soak in — imperfectly, which is one reason models sometimes make things up.

cards.statement: Most pretraining text is labeled by hand by human workers.
cards.why: False. It's overwhelmingly raw text — web pages, books, code, research papers — gathered and filtered by programs. Hand-written human examples matter much more later, in post-training.

cards.title: What the model reads — and what gets thrown away

steps.p: Most training text comes from the public web. Programs called crawlers hop from link to link, saving every page. A free archive, Common Crawl, has stored billions of pages since 2008.

visual.caption: Crawlers follow links and save what they find.

steps.p: Raw web text is full of spam, menus, adverts and gibberish. Labs filter it hard and keep only a small, clean fraction.

items: Remove copies of the same page
A smaller, clean pile to train on

steps.p: The same text — licences, famous quotes, copied articles — appears thousands of times online. Copies are removed, because rereading them teaches little and pushes the model to memorise word for word.
steps.analogy: Revising from one page photocopied 500 times teaches you far less than 500 different pages.

steps.p: Labs decide how much of the mix is web pages, code, maths, books and other languages. More code makes a better programmer; more maths, a better problem-solver.
steps.analogy: Like a diet: what the model "eats" shapes what it's good at.

steps.p: Any text containing the questions from AI tests (benchmarks) is removed, so a high score means real skill rather than having seen the answers.
steps.analogy: Making sure a student hasn't seen the exam paper the night before.

cards.aside: Many researchers now think choosing good data matters as much as the model's design.

cards.q: Why do labs remove duplicate pages from training data?
options: Repeats teach little and push the model to memorise text word for word
Duplicate pages are illegal to use
Computers can't store two copies of the same page
Duplicates make chatting with the model slower
cards.hint: What happens if you read the same page 500 times?
cards.why: Wasted effort and memorising. Seeing one passage hundreds of times teaches almost nothing new, and makes the model likelier to repeat it word for word — bad for both quality and copyright.

cards.statement: Most of what labs download from the web ends up in the final training data.
cards.why: False. Filters throw away most of it: spam, menus, near-copies and low-quality pages. What's left is a much smaller, cleaner slice.

cards.title: Small models trained on carefully chosen "textbook-quality" data can beat much bigger ones.
cards.detail: Microsoft's 2023 paper "Textbooks Are All You Need" trained a coding model with 1.3 billion parameters mostly on filtered and AI-written teaching material. It rivalled models many times its size.

cards.q: What do people mean by the "data wall"?
options: The worry that good human-written text will run out as models need ever more
A firewall that blocks web crawlers
The physical walls of a data center
A limit on how long a prompt can be
cards.hint: Think about supply and demand — for text.
cards.why: Running out of good text. Each generation of models wants several times more data. Researchers such as Epoch AI estimate the stock of quality public text could be used up around the late 2020s, so labs are turning to AI-made (synthetic) data and other sources.

cards.q: What can go wrong if models are trained mostly on text written by earlier AI models?
options: They gradually lose variety and forget rare things
They get much smarter with every round
They start writing only in computer code
Nothing — AI text is identical to human text
cards.hint: Think of a photocopy of a photocopy.
cards.why: They lose variety. A 2024 Nature paper showed that training each generation on the last one's output narrows what models produce; unusual, rare cases fade first. Mixing real human data back in helps.

items: Model 1 copies it, a bit blander

cards.statement: Removing test questions from training data is meant to keep benchmark scores honest.
cards.why: True. If a model has read the exact test questions, a high score might just be memory. Removing them (called decontamination) makes scores a fairer measure of skill.

cards.title: Bigger means better — and you can predict by how much

steps.p: You can make a model better by turning up three things: its size (how many parameters), how much it reads (data), and how much computing power you spend training it (compute).
Researchers track loss — a number for how badly the model predicts the next word. Lower loss means better guesses.
steps.analogy: Like golf: the lower your score, the better you're playing.

steps.p: In 2020, OpenAI researchers found that every time you multiply compute by 10, loss falls by a similar, predictable amount. No sudden walls — one smooth trend over a huge range.

visual.caption: Illustration: every 10× more compute buys a similar drop in loss.

steps.p: These charts use log scales: each step along the axis is ten times the last (1, 10, 100, 1,000…). On them the trend looks almost like a straight line. That pattern is called a power law.
steps.analogy: Like the Richter scale for earthquakes: each step up is 10× bigger.

steps.p: Because the trend is so regular, labs train small, cheap models first, draw the line through them, and extend it to forecast how a huge model will do — before spending tens of millions of dollars.

cards.aside: Loss is predictable. Exactly which skills appear at a given loss is much harder to forecast.

cards.q: On a scaling chart, each step along the bottom is 10× more compute, and the trend is a straight line going down. What does that tell you?
options: Each 10× more compute buys a similar improvement
Doubling compute doubles the model's intelligence
Improvement stops after the first step
Compute makes no difference to quality
cards.hint: Read it as: every step right → the same drop down.
cards.why: Steady returns per 10×. A straight line on a log-scale chart means each 10-fold increase gives about the same gain. That's encouraging (it keeps working) and sobering (each gain costs 10× more).

cards.statement: OpenAI predicted GPT-4's final loss in advance, using much smaller training runs.
cards.why: True. The GPT-4 report says its final loss was predicted from models trained with up to 10,000× less compute. Scaling laws turned a giant bet into something closer to a forecast.

cards.title: In 2022, DeepMind showed most big models had been "under-read": too big for the amount of text they'd seen.
cards.detail: Its 70-billion-parameter model Chinchilla, trained on 1.4 trillion tokens, beat the 280-billion-parameter Gopher using the same compute. The rule of thumb: about 20 tokens of text per parameter.

visual.caption: Same training budget. Smaller model, more reading.

cards.q: With Chinchilla's rule of about 20 tokens per parameter, how much text should a 10-billion-parameter model train on?
options: About 200 billion tokens
About 20 billion tokens
About 2 trillion tokens
About 10 billion tokens
cards.why: About 200 billion. 10 billion × 20 = 200 billion tokens. That split between size and reading gives the best result for a fixed training budget.

cards.statement: Many modern small models are trained on far more text than Chinchilla's rule suggests.
cards.hint: Think about who pays for training versus for using the model.
cards.why: True. Llama 3's 8-billion-parameter model read about 15 trillion tokens — nearly 2,000 per parameter. Extra training is paid once; a smaller, smarter model is cheaper every single time someone uses it.

cards.title: Whether AI skills appear suddenly as models grow is still debated.
cards.detail: Some abilities seem to jump from almost zero to good at a certain size. A 2023 paper argued much of this comes from all-or-nothing scoring: measured with partial credit, progress often looks gradual.

cards.title: What a months-long training run is actually like

steps.p: A frontier model trains on thousands to tens of thousands of GPUs working together for weeks or months. Each handles a slice of the work, and they constantly swap results.
steps.analogy: A stadium full of people each doing part of one enormous sum, shouting results to each other.

steps.p: Each update nudges the model's numbers by an amount set by the learning rate. Too big and training goes haywire; too small and it barely moves.
steps.analogy: Walking downhill in fog: giant leaps send you off a cliff, baby steps take forever.

steps.p: Runs start with tiny steps, ramp up to full size, then gradually shrink the steps toward the end so the model settles into a good spot.

visual.caption: A typical schedule: quick warm-up, then a slow decline.

steps.p: Sometimes loss suddenly jumps up. The team rewinds to a saved snapshot (a checkpoint), changes something — skips the troublesome data or lowers the step size — and carries on.
With tens of thousands of chips, something fails every few hours. Saving checkpoints often means a crash costs minutes of progress, not weeks.
steps.analogy: Like saving your game often, because you know the power will cut out.

cards.aside: Big training runs are as much an operations job as a research one.

cards.q: Why do training runs start with very small update steps (a "warm-up")?
options: Early on the model is random, and big steps can make training blow up
To let the GPUs physically warm up
To save electricity at the start
Because the data hasn't finished downloading
cards.hint: Think: walking in thick fog when you've only just arrived.
cards.why: Stability. At the start the model's numbers are random and its updates are wild. Small steps first stop it from lurching somewhere it can't recover from.

options: A saved snapshot of the model partway through training
A test the model must pass to keep training
A security check on the training data
The final, finished model
cards.why: A save point. Teams save the model's numbers regularly. After a crash or a loss spike, they rewind to the last checkpoint instead of starting over.

cards.title: Meta's 54-day training run for its biggest Llama 3 model was interrupted 466 times.
cards.detail: 419 of those were unexpected, on a cluster of about 16,000 H100 GPUs. Most were hardware faults — failing GPUs and their memory were the top causes.

visual.caption: Interruptions in 54 days — about one every 3 hours.

cards.statement: Loss spikes during training are always caused by bad data.
cards.hint: Think about the step size too.
cards.why: False. A step size that's too big, number-rounding problems and other instabilities can cause them too. Fixes include rewinding, lowering the learning rate, or small changes to the model's design.

cards.q: Big training runs typically use what share of their GPUs' theoretical top speed?
options: About 40%
About 5%
About 95%
Over 100%
cards.hint: Chips spend a lot of time waiting for data to arrive.
cards.why: Roughly 35–45%. Llama 3 reported about 38–43%. The rest is lost to waiting: for data to arrive from memory, and for GPUs to swap results with each other.

cards.statement: Training a top AI model can cost tens of millions of dollars in computing alone.
cards.why: True. Renting thousands of GPUs for months adds up fast. Estimates for frontier models run from tens to hundreds of millions of dollars — which is why labs forecast results with scaling laws first.
